articles.title: Footage of Tibet floods is being heavily censored in China - and we know little about victims there
articles.summary: Some of the most dramatic footage from the deadly flash flooding is hidden from public view in China.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: China censors videos showing deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border By Laura Bicker China correspondent ,  Reporting from Beijing 
- Published 28 August 2026 Updated 29 August 2026 
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives. 
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world. 
Except here, in China. 
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin. 
It has also been difficult to find the full video on China's heavily censored internet. Although various aspects of the disaster have been discussed online. 
But what is even harder to find is any first-hand accounts of survivors describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday. 
- 
Follow live updates 
Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts. 
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever. 
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party. 
China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist. 
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this. 
Figure caption, 
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border 
There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing. 
On Saturday, new footage from Chinese state media showed rescue teams wandering in a wasteland of mud and rock while calling out to anyone trapped. 
But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath. 
We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times. 
As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa. 
Image source, Reuters 
On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works". 
Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled. 
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts. 
Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save. 
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned. 
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster. 
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability. 
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it. 
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role. 
Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith. 
Image source, Gongga Laisong/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images 
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide. 
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents. 
The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable". 
It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists. 
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives. 
The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties". 
To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region. 
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us. 
They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long. 
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country. 
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now. 
Correction 31 August: The headline of this article has been changed to reflect that some footage of the floods is being shown in China, although it is being heavily censored

articles.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: Hundreds have died and thousands are missing after Wednesday's flooding and landslides on the border of Nepal and Tibet.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border By Olivia Ireland ,  Henry Moore   and   Amy Walker 
- Published 26 August 2026 Updated 31 August 2026 
Devastating landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead and thousands more missing. 
At least 794 people have died and more than 2,500 people remain unaccounted for, according to Nepal Police and the country's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. 
At least 16 people have died in Tibet, with another 546 reported missing by Chinese state media. 
On Wednesday, flood water tore through the border region, sweeping away homes and roads, local officials have said. 
Rescue workers say they now face a critical moment to reach remaining survivors as fears mount of further flooding in the disaster's aftermath. 
Here is what we know so far. 
- 
Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood 
- Published 5 days ago 
- 
She was about to cross into Tibet for a long-awaited pilgrimage - then her messages stopped 
- Published 4 days ago 
- 
Follow live updates 
What caused the landslide? 
Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating floods early on Wednesday. 
However, the US Geological Survey (USGS) later confirmed that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse" - when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates. 
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to the agency, causing "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream". 
Powerful flood water and debris travelled some 62 miles (100km) downstream from the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi Rivers, the USGS said, sweeping through towns popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims in northern Nepal. 
Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles as people fled in the Nuwakot region. 
In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuwagadhi Border checkpoint, a multi-storey building on the Nepalese side. 
Gyirong Port, over the border, was also hit. A number of deaths were reported in Tibetan villages. 
Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. 
"I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, [which] dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: What caused the Nepal-Tibet flash floods? 
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of debris that washed into the river systems. 
The ICIMOD said it was assessing whether the Trishuli River had been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If this is the case, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood. 
Separately, China has warned there was a "high risk" a lake that formed after the landslide may burst its banks, causing fresh flooding downstream. As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. 
State media reported that rescue operations were briefly suspended on Friday after the lake, which has formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, overflowed - before water levels dropped slightly. Heavy rain is forecast over the next few days. 
But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain naturally over time. 
A second lake has formed in Tibet after a landslide occurred downstream of the existing so-called barrier lake, Chinese state media reported on Sunday. 
This body of water is also being assessed by experts. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: The lake prompting fears of second flood in Nepal 
How many people are dead and missing? 
The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. 
At least 794 people had died as of Sunday and 2,502 are still missing, according to the country's disaster agency. 
The government has released a list of more than 261 foreign nationals who have been out of contact since the floods hit. 
Meanwhile, 16 people have died in Tibet and 546 are missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV has reported. These figures have not been independently verified and it is unclear whether any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice. 
Tibet, which China annexed in the 1950s, is one of the most strictly controlled regions in the country. It is virtually impossible for foreign media to gain entry there and trying to contact local residents is just as hard. 
Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, a spokesman for Nepal's army, told the BBC that rain and unpredictable weather in the area were making rescue operations increasingly challenging. 
Which countries are the missing tourists from? 
Figure caption, 
Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border 
Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Reports of those missing include the following: 
- 
India - at least 320 Indian nationals are missing, the foreign ministry in Delhi says 
- 
China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal 
- 
US - 90 Americans are still missing, the US state department says 
- 
Ukraine - 62 Ukrainian nationals are missing, Nepalese police say 
- 
Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say 
- 
Australia - 41 Australians are unaccounted for, according to the country's assistant immigration minister 
- 
UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing; Chinese state broadcaster CCTV also reports 15 British nationals are among the missing in Tibet - it is unclear how many of those are included in the figure reported by Nepal 
- 
Canada - 30 Canadians are missing, says the country's foreign ministry 
Smaller numbers of travellers from countries including South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand have also been reported missing. 
How are governments responding? 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Police officers were pictured carrying a survivor from the flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district 
As of midday Sunday, 8,730 people have been rescued, according to Nepal's disaster agency. 
Nepal's priority is to locate the missing and provide urgent relief, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said on Saturday. 
He said authorities were co-ordinating with families to identify those missing, and diplomats were facilitating communications with the relatives of missing foreign nationals. 
He said the risk of possible secondary flooding was being monitored, with officials on "high alert". 
Additional personnel were deployed on Friday in the hopes of speeding up recovery efforts, the office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah said. 
Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting of officials to co-ordinate rescue efforts the same day, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. 
Kamal Kishore, special representative of the UN secretary general for disaster risk reduction, urged countries to support response efforts. 
The US previously promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid for communities affected by the floods, while the UK said it had offered £5m. 
Meanwhile, the Indian Air Force said that military cargo planes carrying nearly 50 tonnes of supplies had been sent to Nepal. 
Might climate change have played a role? 
Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. 
Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding could have been caused by glacial activity – said glacial thinning caused by global warming could increase the risk of landslides. 
But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, told the BBC. 
Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, said that climate change "could have an impact". 
He said his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occurred. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km west of the site of the floods - had collapsed. 
Cook estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream. 
He told the BBC that "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".

articles.title: River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC
articles.summary: Major efforts to rescue hydropower workers continue as Nepal's death toll exceeds 1,000.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Pemba Dundu Tamang tells the BBC how he discovered some of his colleagues were missing after he escaped a flooded tunnel By Ashok Dahal and Kamal Pariyar BBC Nepali ,  Reporting from Nuwakot, central Nepal 
- Published 7 hours ago 
Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week. 
It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining. 
The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away. 
"I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it." 
Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing. 
A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation. 
"We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency. 
"Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease." 
The army said 119 people had been rescued on Tuesday. 
Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill. 
"I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly." 
His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted. 
Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project. 
The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid. 
There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out. 
But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation. 
"I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone." 
Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit. 
Only his wife, son and one nephew survived. 
"I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says. 
"The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer." 
Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die." 
The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived. 
Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive." 
Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them. 
He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Rescue workers are operating at affected hydropower sites to try to find trapped workers 
He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place. 
This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives. 
Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. 
These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable. 
The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say. 
But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives. 
Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites. 
"There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says. 
"I know many people who are still trapped there."

articles.title: The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border
articles.summary: More than 100 Indians are missing at a vital Nepal-China trade crossing after devastating Himalayan floods.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border By Soutik Biswas ,  India correspondent   and   Phanindra Dahal ,  BBC Nepali ,  Reporting from Kathmandu 
- Published 1 September 2026, 07:02 BST 
The video lasts only seconds. 
A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The CCTV footage, whose timestamp reads 10:59:53, went viral. 
For many, it was the first visual evidence of the sheer scale of the destruction that was unfolding. 
What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery show much of the border complex swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone. 
Electronic immigration records from Nepal's Rasuwagadhi border post are filling some gaps, as well as insights from its only surviving staff member. Tika Ram Pokharel, who happened to be in Kathmandu sitting an exam on the day, tells the BBC the crossing was unusually busy when floodwater hit. 
Image source, Satellite image (c) 2026 Vantor Image caption, 
A satellite image shows the area around the Nepal-China border before devastating floods swept away buildings and vehicles 
"This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet," explains Kathmandu-based hydrologist Ajay Dixit. "The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders." 
It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border. 
On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. 
Nepal's immigration department has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster. 
Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal. 
Image source, SOCIAL MEDIA/via REUTERS Image caption, 
CCTV footage shows people fleeing as mud and water engulf buildings at the Nepal-China border in Gyirong on 26 August 
The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 08:35:03 local time (10:52 Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong. 
Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing. 
Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy. 
Tika Ram Pokharel, the surviving senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning. 
The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure, a small trading settlement clustered around the crossing. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing. 
The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing. 
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
Flooding in Rasuwagadhi destroyed the Friendship Bridge, roads and a hydropower substation, and swept away vehicles in Rasuwa, Nepal, last July 
When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area. 
"Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel tells the BBC. 
Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. 
Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together. 
That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck. 
At 08:37 - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood. 
China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes. 
Image caption, 
Tika Ram Pokharel, senior immigration assistant at the Rasuwagadhi Immigration Office, was the only staff member to survive. He was in Kathmandu for an exam when the floods struck 
People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear. 
And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices. 
It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day. 
"My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. 
Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
More than 100 Indians may have been at the crossing when the flood struck. At least 275 remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. 
The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away. 
For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open. 
Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. 
Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped. 
Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area. 
Image source, China News Service/VCG via Getty Images Image caption, 
Rescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong 
When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins." 
The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge. 
Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult. 
Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese. 
Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China. 
Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour. 
Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China. 
Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed , external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. 
The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network. 
"Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. 
"We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port." 
Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing. 
The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck. 
"But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people By Lyse Doucet Chief international correspondent ,  Reporting from Torkham crossing and Kabul 
- Published 1 September 2026, 06:00 BST 
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind. 
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan. 
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins. 
"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags. 
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran. 
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world. 
Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021. 
Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt. 
The expulsions show no sign of stopping. 
Image source, AFP Image caption, 
Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border 
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR. 
"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan. 
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border. 
It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go. 
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all. 
"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry. 
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. 
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing 
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan. 
The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". 
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden. 
The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants". 
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025. 
The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel". 
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified". 
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in". 
Image caption, 
Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone 
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. 
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university? 
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried." 
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified. 
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. 
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside." 
He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work. 
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. 
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights. 
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN. 
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000. 
Image caption, 
Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run Afghanistan 
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face. 
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan." 
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. 
The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition. 
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive. 
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support". 
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve. 
The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule. 
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. 
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?" 
He answers his own question: "Nothing." 
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. 
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

articles.title: Shein valued at $26bn after long-awaited stock market debut
articles.summary: The firm's Hong Kong listing on Tuesday comes after a years-long quest to sell shares in New York and London.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Shein's founder Xu Yangtian, right, and the firm's financial director Poppy Bao at the Hong Kong Stock Exchange By Osmond Chia   and   Emer Moreau ,  Business reporters 
- Published 31 August 2026 Updated 1 September 2026 11:01 BST 
Ultra-fast-fashion brand Shein has been valued at $26.2bn (£19.3bn) after its first day of public trading, following a long quest to list on the stock market. 
The company was once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn, but has faced heated competition, trade tensions and questions over the ethics of its supply chain. 
Shein's share price fell in the early hours of trading but recovered ground before closing down just 0.12%. 
The company's attempts to list in the UK and US were scuppered after supply chain concerns and criticism of its environmental impact. 
On Monday, Shein priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, raising ‌13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars ($1.7bn; £1.3bn) from the listing. 
That gave the company a stock market valuation of $26.3bn. 
Shein's shares fell by as much as 10% in early trading before the losses eased. They closed at $48.50, leaving it valued at $26.15bn. 
Shein became hugely popular , especially among younger people, due to its ability to source the very latest fashions at ultra-low prices through a vast network of factories in China . 
At a ceremony to celebrate the listing, chief financial officer Leigh Gui said the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide. 
"Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion," he said after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading. 
Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed a total of more than a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026, the firm said in a filing ahead of the listing . 
But it now faces higher costs, regulatory scrutiny and more competition, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. 
For customers, the slump in Shein's shares is a sign that the firm's cheap prices are "becoming harder to sustain", which may lead to higher prices, she added. 
A benchmark for fast fashion 
The listing marks the largest new share sale in Hong Kong so far this year, which is being seen as a test of investor appetite for the fast-fashion industry. 
It is a rare "standalone" e-commerce firm that can be assessed on its own merits, fashion industry analyst Louise Deglise-Favre from research firm GlobalData. 
Shares in rivals Asos and Boohoo have been battered in recent years as they face regulatory scrutiny and fierce competition. 
"Investors have learned to be sceptical," while concerns over sustainability and ethical issues add to the complexity of Shein's share sale, Deglise-Favre said. 
- 
The rise and rise of fashion giant Shein 
- Published 7 June 2024 
- 
The truth behind your $12 dress: Inside the Chinese factories fuelling Shein's success 
- Published 12 January 2025 
Founded in China and headquartered in Singapore since 2021, Shein has spent several years touting its credentials as a global company, but ultimately was forced to return to its Asian roots to go public. 
The company once looked set for one of the largest stock market debuts ever by a Chinese firm, with Wall Street in its sights. 
The firm's long road to the stock market highlights the geopolitical pressures and regulatory scrutiny faced by Chinese companies with global ambitions. 
Its business had surged during the Covid-19 pandemic as people, stuck at home, turned to online retailers. At the same time, social media influencers shared their hauls for millions of followers to see. 
Shein faced resistance from US lawmakers, who objected to the planned listing over concerns of forced labour in its factories. In response to such allegations, the company has said it takes a "zero-tolerance policy for forced labour". 
An initial public offering (IPO) in the US - by far Shein's largest market - would have offered it a chance to further increase its global profile and tap into Western financing. 
It has also been accused of copying other designers' ideas. Shein has said "it takes all claims of infringement seriously" and that it respects the rights of all designers. 
Shein also explored the possibility of making its stock market debut in London but faced similar opposition. 
The BBC has contacted Shein for further comment. 
'Only realistic path' 
In 2025, Shein shifted its attention to Hong Kong, with Chinese authorities approving the move in July this year. 
"Shein ran out of venues that could take it," said Ashley Dudarenok, founder of Chinese market research firm ChoZan. 
The company attempted to "look less Chinese" by shifting its headquarters to Singapore ahead of its IPO bid, but it never won political backing abroad nor assurances from Beijing, she added. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Shein is backed by a vast network of factories in China 
Headwinds ahead 
Trade tensions and regulatory concerns mean Shein is navigating a very different landscape to when it first started exploring a potential IPO. 
In July, it reported a $99m quarterly loss as its sales slowed after the US struck down an import duty exemption on small packages. 
The exemption, known as the de minimis rule , had helped Shein and rival Temu grow rapidly as it allowed packages worth less than $800 to enter the US without incurring import duties. 
Similarly, the European Union has imposed a €3 (£2.57; $3.50) tax on low-value imports. 
The Iran war has also hit demand, raised costs and caused delays to deliveries in some markets, Shein has said. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Shein's fast-fashion model has come under scrutiny over its environmental impact 
Its rivals are feeling the pressure too. In August, Temu-owner PDD reported lower-than-expected quarterly revenue. 
The company also needs to find ways to stand out from its rivals, that are now also using predictive technology to make their websites more appealing to shoppers, said Jason Hsu from Rayliant Global Advisors. 
"Shein is no longer a unique player," Hsu said. 
Shein is also being investigated by US and European regulators over its business practices.

articles.title: Nepal death toll crosses 1,000 as rescuers race to find workers trapped in mud-filled tunnels
articles.summary: Thousands are still missing as Chinese state media report the official number of fatalities in Tibet at 16.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images By Jake Lapham ,  Kelly Ng   and   BBC Nepali 
- Published 31 August 2026 Updated 1 September 2026 08:37 BST 
The death toll in Nepal from devastating floods on the border with Tibet has crossed 1,000, according to the country's disaster agency. 
More than 3,900 people remain missing - of whom more than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River. 
Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels - and while a team did manage to gain entry to one of them, it withdrew after finding no-one there. 
"I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali. 
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites. 
The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved. 
Image source, Nepal Army/Reuters Image caption, 
Army personnel have resorted to using explosives to blast into the hillside to reach the trapped workers 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Each hydropower plant employs hundreds of workers, including local and migrant labourers and high-skilled engineers 
"I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur. 
Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said. 
Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier. 
A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but retreated after no one was found there. 
"The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur. 
"It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added. 
Rescue operations had been "intensified", Nepalese leader Shah said, noting that the floods were "not an ordinary" event. 
"This incident indicates that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change. 
"It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change," Shah wrote in a Facebook post late on Monday. 
Another family member anxiously awaiting news is Priya Kharel, whose brother Milan was working as an engineer in the Upper Trishuli-1 plant when the floods hit. 
"Those who returned from the hydropower site said there were people inside the tunnel," she told BBC News Nepali. "So there is hope that if the army reaches them quickly, they can be saved." 
Australian engineer Arnold Dix, who has been helping Nepalese authorities with the underground search operations remotely, said rescuers had been struggling to find the tunnels. 
"The actual signature of them has gone – everything is just missing. It looks like a lunar landscape," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One. 
Once rescuers knew where the power stations were, Dix said they could then decide the best way to access them, which typically involves digging and "blasting boulders". 
"There's boulders bigger than houses. I've never seen that before in my life. It's just an extraordinary operation," the former head of the International Tunnelling Association said. 
He said he still has some hope for those trapped underground, given the protection the subterranean environment might have offered from the deluge above. 
Figure caption, 
Once a village, now barren land - BBC in valley devastated by floods 
Only 4% of the 900 bodies that have been found so far have been identified, a spokesperson from the Ministry of Health told BBC Nepali. 
In Chitwan, a district far downstream from where the floods first hit, makeshift burials were taking place after the Himalayan nation's river systems brought nearly 300 dead bodies to its banks. 
The air was thick with the smell of decay, as men wearing white Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including masks carried unidentified corpses into trucks. 
Over the weekend, a large portion of the forest outside the city was dug up. Medical staff and volunteers worked to extract DNA from the unidentified remains. 
Ganesh Aryaal, the chief district officer, told BBC Nepali that relatives will still be able to extricate the remains of their loved ones, once they are identified through DNA testing. 
"We don't have enough freezers here... We had to choose this last alternative of temporary burial system. We are really overwhelmed," he said. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Authorities in Chitwan have resorted to burying unidentified bodies 
In Tibet, the Chinese-appointed Panchen Lama - who is the second-highest spiritual leader in Tibetan Buddhism - held a memorial service as search teams continued to wade through waist-high mud. 
The official death toll on the Tibetan side is 16, with 546 reported missing, according to Chinese state media. Footage of the floods has been heavily censored in China. 
The base of a single water tower is the only structure still standing in the once bustling border crossing with Nepal, state media report. 
Chinese authorities have imposed "administrative penalties" – which can range from warnings and fines to short detentions – on people speculating online that the casualty numbers are a lot higher than reported. 
In Nepal, authorities have also ordered the removal of online content that they deem to be misinformation about the floods.

articles.title: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
articles.summary: Japanese companies are doubling down on India amid a shrinking domestic market and rising risks in China.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Brands like Uniqlo and Muji have rapidly expanded in India By Nikhil Inamdar Mumbai 
- Published 31 August 2026 
India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent. 
If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India. 
Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding. 
Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson , external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai. 
It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets. 
MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector. 
Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake. 
Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific. 
More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report , external . GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs. 
"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200m fund in India, told the BBC. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments in India through some 120 agreements during PM Sanae Takaichi's visit in July 
At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says. 
"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited." 
Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth. 
Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago. 
After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology. 
But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle. 
At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments. They signed around 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. In fact, Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country. 
Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal. 
Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India. 
The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently , external , is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India". 
But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC. 
India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says. 
"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
India's consumer market is growing fast as discretionary incomes rise 
For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time. 
India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai. 
But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts. 
"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll , external . 
"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China." 
Also, India remains a tough country to do business. 
Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese. 
An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed , external . 
Chinese state media , external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts. 
It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.
